Phase 1 — AI Engineering Spine (Weeks 1–11)   

The first eleven weeks are the AI Engineering Spine — this is where you build the actual technical foundation, one layer at a time. 
Week one is Agentic AI Foundations: you start from the core mental model we use for the rest of the program — an agent equals prompt plus tools plus memory, multiplied by the LLM — and the ReAct loop, thought, action, observation, repeat. You ship your first live project in week one itself: an LLM-powered CRM lead qualifier agent. 
Weeks two and three move into RAG-Powered Knowledge Agents — real retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, not toy demos, and critically, how to actually measure whether a RAG system is good: precision at K, recall at K, groundedness, hallucination prevention. Live project: an end-to-end grounded IT support knowledge assistant.
Week four is Multi-Agent Systems — once a task gets complex enough, one agent isn't enough, so you learn role-based design and orchestration using LangGraph, building a multi-agent travel planner. Week five is Conversational and Multimodal Agents — voice architectures, both cascaded and real-time speech-to-speech, plus human-in-the-loop patterns, where a system pauses for a human to review before acting, which matters enormously the moment you're inside a real enterprise. Live project: a voice-enabled e-commerce assistant with human-in-the-loop approval. And week six is genuinely advanced material: Agent Communication Protocols — MCP, A2A, ACP — how agents actually talk to each other reliably, using the Model Context Protocol and Google's Agent Development Kit. Live project: a real estate negotiation simulator, with a buyer agent and a seller agent actually negotiating against each other.
Week seven is Hybrid Search and Retrieval — sparse versus dense vectors, combining both through reciprocal rank fusion, hands-on with a real e-commerce product dataset. Week eight — and I'd call this one of the most important weeks in the entire program — is Agent Observability, Evaluation, and Safety. This is what separates a demo from something an enterprise will actually trust in production: tracing every agent decision, building evaluation datasets, guardrails, PII detection and redaction for GDPR and HIPAA patterns, and cost control. Live project: a production-ready fintech support agent. And week nine is Fine-Tuning and Domain Adaptation — when you actually need to fine-tune a model versus just improving a prompt or a RAG pipeline, and then doing it, on free compute, and deploying it. Live project: a domain-specific fine-tuned healthcare Q&A agent.
And weeks ten and eleven are your first capstone build — a full enterprise multi-agent system, over two weeks, where you own the problem definition, the architecture, every trade-off, and the final review. It's instructor-supported, but it's genuinely your system, reviewed the way a real enterprise agentic system gets reviewed in production. We'll come back to what you can actually build here in a minute.

Phase 2 — AI-Assisted Coding (Week 12)  
Week twelve is one deliberately focused week: pair programming with Claude. It sits right before the FDE-specific weeks on purpose, because from this point forward, you're expected to build fast using AI-assisted coding tools — specifically Claude Code, using a five-phase framework we teach you. This isn't a nice-to-have elective. It's a prerequisite for how the rest of the program actually runs.

Phase 3 — FDE Spine (Weeks 13–17)   
Weeks thirteen through seventeen are the FDE Spine — this is where the program stops being general AI engineering and becomes specifically the FDE craft. Primary stack across these weeks is OpenAI's Agents SDK plus AWS Bedrock Agentcore, with an alternate-stack option using Google ADK and Vertex AI, or Claude's Agent SDK and Azure — so you're not locked into thinking in just one vendor's world.

Week thirteen is Customer Discovery and Scoping — and this is also exactly when your FDE capstone engagement starts. You learn the actual FDE lifecycle, scope, build, deploy, operate, how to run a discovery workshop, stakeholder mapping and RACI, and how to frame a problem with success criteria anchored to evaluation metrics, not vibes. 
Week fourteen is Statement of Work, Pricing, and Solution Architecture — genuinely rare content. Most engineering programs never teach you how to estimate a project, write a defensible SoW, or understand pricing models like time-and-materials-with-a-cap versus fixed-price versus outcome-based. There's a live procurement interrogation drill built into this week.
Week fifteen, Building Production Agents, is the deep technical week — OpenAI's Agents SDK, handoffs, guardrails, sessions, CI/CD with evaluation gates that actually block a bad deploy, and hardening for multi-tenant production environments. Week sixteen is APIs, MCP Servers, and RBAC — the real plumbing of enterprise integration: REST, webhooks, batch and streaming, OAuth2, building and hardening your own MCP servers, and role-based access control end to end. Live project: a real multi-tenant MCP server integrated with at least two systems.
And week seventeen, Evals, Observability, and Handover, is also when your FDE capstone gets completed. Data governance and compliance — SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR — evaluation suites as a CI deploy gate, SLAs and SLOs, incident response, and how you actually hand a finished system off to the customer's own team with a proper runbook. This is the week that directly answers the ‘will it still be running after you leave’ fear we talked about back in chapter three.

Once the technical foundation is established, the next five weeks focus on the FDE Craft.
This is the layer that differentiates a Forward Deployed Engineer from a traditional AI Engineer.
Most professionals already possess some technical or domain expertise, but they may not have worked in a deeply customer-facing engineering role.
Here, you learn how to enter an ambiguous customer environment, conduct discovery, identify the real business problem, define success criteria and translate the problem into a phased technical plan.
You work through the complete FDE lifecycle:
Discovery, scoping, solution architecture, integration, building, evaluation, deployment, handover and ongoing improvement.
You also learn how to work with the customer’s existing systems and data, manage technical and business stakeholders, push back on unrealistic requirements and connect engineering decisions to measurable enterprise outcomes.

Very very important - 
These are not merely customer-management concepts.
Experienced FDE practitioners teach this section through real case studies, role-playing, customer simulations and FDE-focused projects. You practise solving ambiguous problems involving real constraints, messy systems and incomplete requirements.
This remains an engineering-first approach. The FDE does not stop at recommending the architecture; they participate in building and deploying the solution.

Why does this actually need a structured program rather than self-study? 
Five shifts have to happen: from tool demos to production systems. 
From just using AI to real engineering judgment.
 From traditional engineering habits to actual FDE craft. 
From generic interview prep to interview prep built for this specific loop.

Honestly — the FDE-specific options in India right now are either purely academic tracks or scattered self-serve content. A live cohort that actually combines all three layers — AI engineering, solutioning, and interview readiness — doesn't really exist here yet. That's the specific gap we built this program to close.

Phase 4 — FDE Interview Prep (Weeks 18–23)  
Weeks eighteen through twenty-four are FDE-specific interview preparation — and I want to be direct about this, it is not generic DSA prep repackaged. Each week is built around a category of system you'll actually be asked to reason about live, in a real FDE interview loop. Week eighteen is Agentic Research Systems — designing an agent that plans, uses tools, and doesn't hallucinate its research, with source verification built in. Week nineteen is Agentic Text-to-SQL — reliable data reasoning, and specifically, how you prevent an agent from ever running a dangerous query against a real production database.
Week twenty is Multi-Agent Coordination — how agents actually communicate and delegate, and critically, how a multi-agent system knows when to stop, so it doesn't loop forever or blow up your cost. Week twenty-one is Self-Improving Agents — systems that generate a fix, test it, and refine it, inside a sandboxed environment with rollback.
Week twenty-two is where it gets specifically FDE: Decomposition and Case Study Interviews. This is the single most distinctive round in an FDE interview loop — it originated at Palantir, and today it's used at OpenAI, Anthropic, Glean, Salesforce, and Databricks. You'll work through a library of ten-plus real case scenarios across fintech, healthcare, defense, and enterprise SaaS, and you'll learn the specific ways candidates fail this round — jumping to a solution before framing the problem properly, missing the data picture entirely, not anchoring your scope to actual evals. This week also includes the AI-assisted pair-coding interview round, using Claude Code from week twelve, and a system design round built specifically around agentic and RAG architectures.
Week twenty-three is Behavioral and Procurement-Security Interviews — sixteen FDE-specific behavioral prompts across eight categories: customer disagreement, a live deployment incident, navigating an org chart, escalation moments. And something genuinely unique to this program: a procurement and security simulation, where a hostile ‘security officer’ cross-examines you on data residency, audit trails, vendor risk, prompt-injection mitigation. In a real FDE process, this round exists, and almost nobody walks in prepared for it. The program closes out through week twenty-four with placement support, your final decision-log entry, a portfolio walkthrough, and planning your first ninety days in an actual FDE role.

One framing before the curriculum, because this is what actually gets you hired.

Add personal preparation example -  studying product documentation, research papers and features hands-on before interviewing for an FDE role.

Four layers. Your domain expertise at the bottom - that's what you already walk in with. AI engineering skills on top of that. Then customer solutioning, the FDE craft. And at the very top, a project portfolio.

The bottom three are capability. The top one is where capability becomes proof - something visible and defensible that someone else can look at and assess.

That top layer is the one most people never build. And it's the single biggest reason strong engineers don't convert interviews.

The final six weeks focus on FDE-specific interview preparation.
Having the skills is only one part of the transition. You must also be able to demonstrate them in the format used by FDE hiring teams.
A large component is generally AI or agentic system design.
You may receive a broad problem such as:
“How would you build an AI solution for this customer, in this industry, under these constraints?”
The statement may appear simple, and some constraints may not be provided upfront. That is intentional.
The interviewer is evaluating the questions you ask, how you uncover requirements, how you decompose the problem, the architecture you propose and whether you understand the solution’s limitations, risks and trade-offs.
You also prepare for decomposition rounds and client simulations. These assess how you approach an ambiguous customer problem, define the business outcome, establish KPIs and convert the requirement into a realistic delivery plan.
Behavioural preparation is also included because FDEs work directly with customers and cross-functional stakeholders.
DSA preparation is available based on the companies and roles you plan to target. The DSA requirement for FDEs is generally lighter than a traditional software-engineering interview and is also company-dependent.
By this stage, you have developed the technical capability, customer-facing problem-solving skills, project proof and interview approach required for an FDE transition.

Two: ask us anything. Prerequisites, timelines, what the gap actually looks like for you, the money. Nothing is off-limits on that call.

Phase 1 — AI Engineering Spine (Weeks 1–11)   

The first eleven weeks are the AI Engineering Spine — this is where you build the actual technical foundation, one layer at a time. 
Week one is Agentic AI Foundations: you start from the core mental model we use for the rest of the program — an agent equals prompt plus tools plus memory, multiplied by the LLM — and the ReAct loop, thought, action, observation, repeat. You ship your first live project in week one itself: an LLM-powered CRM lead qualifier agent. 
Weeks two and three move into RAG-Powered Knowledge Agents — real retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, not toy demos, and critically, how to actually measure whether a RAG system is good: precision at K, recall at K, groundedness, hallucination prevention. Live project: an end-to-end grounded IT support knowledge assistant.
Week four is Multi-Agent Systems — once a task gets complex enough, one agent isn't enough, so you learn role-based design and orchestration using LangGraph, building a multi-agent travel planner. Week five is Conversational and Multimodal Agents — voice architectures, both cascaded and real-time speech-to-speech, plus human-in-the-loop patterns, where a system pauses for a human to review before acting, which matters enormously the moment you're inside a real enterprise. Live project: a voice-enabled e-commerce assistant with human-in-the-loop approval. And week six is genuinely advanced material: Agent Communication Protocols — MCP, A2A, ACP — how agents actually talk to each other reliably, using the Model Context Protocol and Google's Agent Development Kit. Live project: a real estate negotiation simulator, with a buyer agent and a seller agent actually negotiating against each other.
Week seven is Hybrid Search and Retrieval — sparse versus dense vectors, combining both through reciprocal rank fusion, hands-on with a real e-commerce product dataset. Week eight — and I'd call this one of the most important weeks in the entire program — is Agent Observability, Evaluation, and Safety. This is what separates a demo from something an enterprise will actually trust in production: tracing every agent decision, building evaluation datasets, guardrails, PII detection and redaction for GDPR and HIPAA patterns, and cost control. Live project: a production-ready fintech support agent. And week nine is Fine-Tuning and Domain Adaptation — when you actually need to fine-tune a model versus just improving a prompt or a RAG pipeline, and then doing it, on free compute, and deploying it. Live project: a domain-specific fine-tuned healthcare Q&A agent.
And weeks ten and eleven are your first capstone build — a full enterprise multi-agent system, over two weeks, where you own the problem definition, the architecture, every trade-off, and the final review. It's instructor-supported, but it's genuinely your system, reviewed the way a real enterprise agentic system gets reviewed in production. We'll come back to what you can actually build here in a minute.

Phase 1 — AI Engineering Spine (Weeks 1–11)   

The first eleven weeks are the AI Engineering Spine — this is where you build the actual technical foundation, one layer at a time. 
Week one is Agentic AI Foundations: you start from the core mental model we use for the rest of the program — an agent equals prompt plus tools plus memory, multiplied by the LLM — and the ReAct loop, thought, action, observation, repeat. You ship your first live project in week one itself: an LLM-powered CRM lead qualifier agent. 
Weeks two and three move into RAG-Powered Knowledge Agents — real retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, not toy demos, and critically, how to actually measure whether a RAG system is good: precision at K, recall at K, groundedness, hallucination prevention. Live project: an end-to-end grounded IT support knowledge assistant.
Week four is Multi-Agent Systems — once a task gets complex enough, one agent isn't enough, so you learn role-based design and orchestration using LangGraph, building a multi-agent travel planner. Week five is Conversational and Multimodal Agents — voice architectures, both cascaded and real-time speech-to-speech, plus human-in-the-loop patterns, where a system pauses for a human to review before acting, which matters enormously the moment you're inside a real enterprise. Live project: a voice-enabled e-commerce assistant with human-in-the-loop approval. And week six is genuinely advanced material: Agent Communication Protocols — MCP, A2A, ACP — how agents actually talk to each other reliably, using the Model Context Protocol and Google's Agent Development Kit. Live project: a real estate negotiation simulator, with a buyer agent and a seller agent actually negotiating against each other.
Week seven is Hybrid Search and Retrieval — sparse versus dense vectors, combining both through reciprocal rank fusion, hands-on with a real e-commerce product dataset. Week eight — and I'd call this one of the most important weeks in the entire program — is Agent Observability, Evaluation, and Safety. This is what separates a demo from something an enterprise will actually trust in production: tracing every agent decision, building evaluation datasets, guardrails, PII detection and redaction for GDPR and HIPAA patterns, and cost control. Live project: a production-ready fintech support agent. And week nine is Fine-Tuning and Domain Adaptation — when you actually need to fine-tune a model versus just improving a prompt or a RAG pipeline, and then doing it, on free compute, and deploying it. Live project: a domain-specific fine-tuned healthcare Q&A agent.
And weeks ten and eleven are your first capstone build — a full enterprise multi-agent system, over two weeks, where you own the problem definition, the architecture, every trade-off, and the final review. It's instructor-supported, but it's genuinely your system, reviewed the way a real enterprise agentic system gets reviewed in production. We'll come back to what you can actually build here in a minute.

Weeks thirteen through seventeen are the FDE Spine — this is where the program stops being general AI engineering and becomes specifically the FDE craft. Phase 1 — AI Engineering Spine (Weeks 1–11)   

The first eleven weeks are the AI Engineering Spine — this is where you build the actual technical foundation, one layer at a time. 
Week one is Agentic AI Foundations: you start from the core mental model we use for the rest of the program — an agent equals prompt plus tools plus memory, multiplied by the LLM — and the ReAct loop, thought, action, observation, repeat. You ship your first live project in week one itself: an LLM-powered CRM lead qualifier agent. 
Weeks two and three move into RAG-Powered Knowledge Agents — real retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, not toy demos, and critically, how to actually measure whether a RAG system is good: precision at K, recall at K, groundedness, hallucination prevention. Live project: an end-to-end grounded IT support knowledge assistant.
Week four is Multi-Agent Systems — once a task gets complex enough, one agent isn't enough, so you learn role-based design and orchestration using LangGraph, building a multi-agent travel planner. Week five is Conversational and Multimodal Agents — voice architectures, both cascaded and real-time speech-to-speech, plus human-in-the-loop patterns, where a system pauses for a human to review before acting, which matters enormously the moment you're inside a real enterprise. Live project: a voice-enabled e-commerce assistant with human-in-the-loop approval. And week six is genuinely advanced material: Agent Communication Protocols — MCP, A2A, ACP — how agents actually talk to each other reliably, using the Model Context Protocol and Google's Agent Development Kit. Live project: a real estate negotiation simulator, with a buyer agent and a seller agent actually negotiating against each other.
Week seven is Hybrid Search and Retrieval — sparse versus dense vectors, combining both through reciprocal rank fusion, hands-on with a real e-commerce product dataset. Week eight — and I'd call this one of the most important weeks in the entire program — is Agent Observability, Evaluation, and Safety. This is what separates a demo from something an enterprise will actually trust in production: tracing every agent decision, building evaluation datasets, guardrails, PII detection and redaction for GDPR and HIPAA patterns, and cost control. Live project: a production-ready fintech support agent. And week nine is Fine-Tuning and Domain Adaptation — when you actually need to fine-tune a model versus just improving a prompt or a RAG pipeline, and then doing it, on free compute, and deploying it. Live project: a domain-specific fine-tuned healthcare Q&A agent.
And weeks ten and eleven are your first capstone build — a full enterprise multi-agent system, over two weeks, where you own the problem definition, the architecture, every trade-off, and the final review. It's instructor-supported, but it's genuinely your system, reviewed the way a real enterprise agentic system gets reviewed in production. Phase 4 — FDE Interview Prep (Weeks 18–23)  
Weeks eighteen through twenty-four are FDE-specific interview preparation — and I want to be direct about this, it is not generic DSA prep repackaged. Each week is built around a category of system you'll actually be asked to reason about live, in a real FDE interview loop. Week eighteen is Agentic Research Systems — designing an agent that plans, uses tools, and doesn't hallucinate its research, with source verification built in. Week nineteen is Agentic Text-to-SQL — reliable data reasoning, and specifically, how you prevent an agent from ever running a dangerous query against a real production database.
Week twenty is Multi-Agent Coordination — how agents actually communicate and delegate, and critically, how a multi-agent system knows when to stop, so it doesn't loop forever or blow up your cost. Week twenty-one is Self-Improving Agents — systems that generate a fix, test it, and refine it, inside a sandboxed environment with rollback.
Week twenty-two is where it gets specifically FDE: Decomposition and Case Study Interviews. This is the single most distinctive round in an FDE interview loop — it originated at Palantir, and today it's used at OpenAI, Anthropic, Glean, Salesforce, and Databricks. You'll work through a library of ten-plus real case scenarios across fintech, healthcare, defense, and enterprise SaaS, and you'll learn the specific ways candidates fail this round — jumping to a solution before framing the problem properly, missing the data picture entirely, not anchoring your scope to actual evals. This week also includes the AI-assisted pair-coding interview round, using Claude Code from week twelve, and a system design round built specifically around agentic and RAG architectures.
Week twenty-three is Behavioral and Procurement-Security Interviews — sixteen FDE-specific behavioral prompts across eight categories: customer disagreement, a live deployment incident, navigating an org chart, escalation moments. And something genuinely unique to this program: a procurement and security simulation, where a hostile ‘security officer’ cross-examines you on data residency, audit trails, vendor risk, prompt-injection mitigation. In a real FDE process, this round exists, and almost nobody walks in prepared for it. The program closes out through week twenty-four with placement support, your final decision-log entry, a portfolio walkthrough, and planning your first ninety days in an actual FDE role.

Week thirteen is Customer Discovery and Scoping — and this is also exactly when your FDE capstone engagement starts. You learn the actual FDE lifecycle, scope, build, deploy, operate, how to run a discovery workshop, stakeholder mapping and RACI, and how to frame a problem with success criteria anchored to evaluation metrics, not vibes. 
Week fourteen is Statement of Work, Pricing, and Solution Architecture — genuinely rare content. Most engineering programs never teach you how to estimate a project, write a defensible SoW, or understand pricing models like time-and-materials-with-a-cap versus fixed-price versus outcome-based. There's a live procurement interrogation drill built into this week.
Week fifteen, Building Production Agents, is the deep technical week — OpenAI's Agents SDK, handoffs, guardrails, sessions, CI/CD with evaluation gates that actually block a bad deploy, and hardening for multi-tenant production environments. Week sixteen is APIs, MCP Servers, and RBAC — the real plumbing of enterprise integration: REST, webhooks, batch and streaming, OAuth2, building and hardening your own MCP servers, and role-based access control end to end. Live project: a real multi-tenant MCP server integrated with at least two systems.
And week seventeen, Evals, Observability, and Handover, is also when your FDE capstone gets completed. Data governance and compliance — SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR — evaluation suites as a CI deploy gate, SLAs and SLOs, incident response, and how you actually hand a finished system off to the customer's own team with a proper runbook. This is the week that directly answers the ‘will it still be running after you leave’ fear we talked about back in chapter three.

Phase 1 — AI Engineering Spine (Weeks 1–11)   

The first eleven weeks are the AI Engineering Spine — this is where you build the actual technical foundation, one layer at a time. 
Week one is Agentic AI Foundations: you start from the core mental model we use for the rest of the program — an agent equals prompt plus tools plus memory, multiplied by the LLM — and the ReAct loop, thought, action, observation, repeat. You ship your first live project in week one itself: an LLM-powered CRM lead qualifier agent. 
Weeks two and three move into RAG-Powered Knowledge Agents — real retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, not toy demos, and critically, how to actually measure whether a RAG system is good: precision at K, recall at K, groundedness, hallucination prevention. Live project: an end-to-end grounded IT support knowledge assistant.
Week four is Multi-Agent Systems — once a task gets complex enough, one agent isn't enough, so you learn role-based design and orchestration using LangGraph, building a multi-agent travel planner. Week five is Conversational and Multimodal Agents — voice architectures, both cascaded and real-time speech-to-speech, plus human-in-the-loop patterns, where a system pauses for a human to review before acting, which matters enormously the moment you're inside a real enterprise. Live project: a voice-enabled e-commerce assistant with human-in-the-loop approval. And week six is genuinely advanced material: Agent Communication Protocols — MCP, A2A, ACP — how agents actually talk to each other reliably, using the Model Context Protocol and Google's Agent Development Kit. Live project: a real estate negotiation simulator, with a buyer agent and a seller agent actually negotiating against each other.
Week seven is Hybrid Search and Retrieval — sparse versus dense vectors, combining both through reciprocal rank fusion, hands-on with a real e-commerce product dataset. Week eight — and I'd call this one of the most important weeks in the entire program — is Agent Observability, Evaluation, and Safety. This is what separates a demo from something an enterprise will actually trust in production: tracing every agent decision, building evaluation datasets, guardrails, PII detection and redaction for GDPR and HIPAA patterns, and cost control. Live project: a production-ready fintech support agent. And week nine is Fine-Tuning and Domain Adaptation — when you actually need to fine-tune a model versus just improving a prompt or a RAG pipeline, and then doing it, on free compute, and deploying it. Live project: a domain-specific fine-tuned healthcare Q&A agent.
And weeks ten and eleven are your first capstone build — a full enterprise multi-agent system, over two weeks, where you own the problem definition, the architecture, every trade-off, and the final review. It's instructor-supported, but it's genuinely your system, reviewed the way a real enterprise agentic system gets reviewed in production. Phase 1 — AI Engineering Spine (Weeks 1–11)   

The first eleven weeks are the AI Engineering Spine — this is where you build the actual technical foundation, one layer at a time. 
Week one is Agentic AI Foundations: you start from the core mental model we use for the rest of the program — an agent equals prompt plus tools plus memory, multiplied by the LLM — and the ReAct loop, thought, action, observation, repeat. You ship your first live project in week one itself: an LLM-powered CRM lead qualifier agent. 
Weeks two and three move into RAG-Powered Knowledge Agents — real retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, not toy demos, and critically, how to actually measure whether a RAG system is good: precision at K, recall at K, groundedness, hallucination prevention. Live project: an end-to-end grounded IT support knowledge assistant.
Week four is Multi-Agent Systems — once a task gets complex enough, one agent isn't enough, so you learn role-based design and orchestration using LangGraph, building a multi-agent travel planner. Week five is Conversational and Multimodal Agents — voice architectures, both cascaded and real-time speech-to-speech, plus human-in-the-loop patterns, where a system pauses for a human to review before acting, which matters enormously the moment you're inside a real enterprise. Live project: a voice-enabled e-commerce assistant with human-in-the-loop approval. And week six is genuinely advanced material: Agent Communication Protocols — MCP, A2A, ACP — how agents actually talk to each other reliably, using the Model Context Protocol and Google's Agent Development Kit. Live project: a real estate negotiation simulator, with a buyer agent and a seller agent actually negotiating against each other.
Week seven is Hybrid Search and Retrieval — sparse versus dense vectors, combining both through reciprocal rank fusion, hands-on with a real e-commerce product dataset. Week eight — and I'd call this one of the most important weeks in the entire program — is Agent Observability, Evaluation, and Safety. This is what separates a demo from something an enterprise will actually trust in production: tracing every agent decision, building evaluation datasets, guardrails, PII detection and redaction for GDPR and HIPAA patterns, and cost control. Live project: a production-ready fintech support agent. And week nine is Fine-Tuning and Domain Adaptation — when you actually need to fine-tune a model versus just improving a prompt or a RAG pipeline, and then doing it, on free compute, and deploying it. Live project: a domain-specific fine-tuned healthcare Q&A agent.
And weeks ten and eleven are your first capstone build — a full enterprise multi-agent system, over two weeks, where you own the problem definition, the architecture, every trade-off, and the final review. It's instructor-supported, but it's genuinely your system, reviewed the way a real enterprise agentic system gets reviewed in production. Phase 1 — AI Engineering Spine (Weeks 1–11)   

The first eleven weeks are the AI Engineering Spine — this is where you build the actual technical foundation, one layer at a time. 
Week one is Agentic AI Foundations: you start from the core mental model we use for the rest of the program — an agent equals prompt plus tools plus memory, multiplied by the LLM — and the ReAct loop, thought, action, observation, repeat. You ship your first live project in week one itself: an LLM-powered CRM lead qualifier agent. 
Weeks two and three move into RAG-Powered Knowledge Agents — real retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, not toy demos, and critically, how to actually measure whether a RAG system is good: precision at K, recall at K, groundedness, hallucination prevention. Live project: an end-to-end grounded IT support knowledge assistant.
Week four is Multi-Agent Systems — once a task gets complex enough, one agent isn't enough, so you learn role-based design and orchestration using LangGraph, building a multi-agent travel planner. Week five is Conversational and Multimodal Agents — voice architectures, both cascaded and real-time speech-to-speech, plus human-in-the-loop patterns, where a system pauses for a human to review before acting, which matters enormously the moment you're inside a real enterprise. Live project: a voice-enabled e-commerce assistant with human-in-the-loop approval. And week six is genuinely advanced material: Agent Communication Protocols — MCP, A2A, ACP — how agents actually talk to each other reliably, using the Model Context Protocol and Google's Agent Development Kit. Live project: a real estate negotiation simulator, with a buyer agent and a seller agent actually negotiating against each other.
Week seven is Hybrid Search and Retrieval — sparse versus dense vectors, combining both through reciprocal rank fusion, hands-on with a real e-commerce product dataset. Week eight — and I'd call this one of the most important weeks in the entire program — is Agent Observability, Evaluation, and Safety. This is what separates a demo from something an enterprise will actually trust in production: tracing every agent decision, building evaluation datasets, guardrails, PII detection and redaction for GDPR and HIPAA patterns, and cost control. Live project: a production-ready fintech support agent. And week nine is Fine-Tuning and Domain Adaptation — when you actually need to fine-tune a model versus just improving a prompt or a RAG pipeline, and then doing it, on free compute, and deploying it. Live project: a domain-specific fine-tuned healthcare Q&A agent.
And weeks ten and eleven are your first capstone build — a full enterprise multi-agent system, over two weeks, where you own the problem definition, the architecture, every trade-off, and the final review. It's instructor-supported, but it's genuinely your system, reviewed the way a real enterprise agentic system gets reviewed in production. Phase 4 — FDE Interview Prep (Weeks 18–23)  
Weeks eighteen through twenty-four are FDE-specific interview preparation — and I want to be direct about this, it is not generic DSA prep repackaged. Phase 1 — AI Engineering Spine (Weeks 1–11)   

The first eleven weeks are the AI Engineering Spine — this is where you build the actual technical foundation, one layer at a time. 
Week one is Agentic AI Foundations: you start from the core mental model we use for the rest of the program — an agent equals prompt plus tools plus memory, multiplied by the LLM — and the ReAct loop, thought, action, observation, repeat. You ship your first live project in week one itself: an LLM-powered CRM lead qualifier agent. 
Weeks two and three move into RAG-Powered Knowledge Agents — real retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, not toy demos, and critically, how to actually measure whether a RAG system is good: precision at K, recall at K, groundedness, hallucination prevention. Live project: an end-to-end grounded IT support knowledge assistant.
Week four is Multi-Agent Systems — once a task gets complex enough, one agent isn't enough, so you learn role-based design and orchestration using LangGraph, building a multi-agent travel planner. Week five is Conversational and Multimodal Agents — voice architectures, both cascaded and real-time speech-to-speech, plus human-in-the-loop patterns, where a system pauses for a human to review before acting, which matters enormously the moment you're inside a real enterprise. Live project: a voice-enabled e-commerce assistant with human-in-the-loop approval. And week six is genuinely advanced material: Agent Communication Protocols — MCP, A2A, ACP — how agents actually talk to each other reliably, using the Model Context Protocol and Google's Agent Development Kit. Live project: a real estate negotiation simulator, with a buyer agent and a seller agent actually negotiating against each other.
Week seven is Hybrid Search and Retrieval — sparse versus dense vectors, combining both through reciprocal rank fusion, hands-on with a real e-commerce product dataset. Week eight — and I'd call this one of the most important weeks in the entire program — is Agent Observability, Evaluation, and Safety. This is what separates a demo from something an enterprise will actually trust in production: tracing every agent decision, building evaluation datasets, guardrails, PII detection and redaction for GDPR and HIPAA patterns, and cost control. Live project: a production-ready fintech support agent. And week nine is Fine-Tuning and Domain Adaptation — when you actually need to fine-tune a model versus just improving a prompt or a RAG pipeline, and then doing it, on free compute, and deploying it. Live project: a domain-specific fine-tuned healthcare Q&A agent.
And weeks ten and eleven are your first capstone build — a full enterprise multi-agent system, over two weeks, where you own the problem definition, the architecture, every trade-off, and the final review. It's instructor-supported, but it's genuinely your system, reviewed the way a real enterprise agentic system gets reviewed in production. Phase 4 — FDE Interview Prep (Weeks 18–23)  
Weeks eighteen through twenty-four are FDE-specific interview preparation — and I want to be direct about this, it is not generic DSA prep repackaged. Each week is built around a category of system you'll actually be asked to reason about live, in a real FDE interview loop. Week eighteen is Agentic Research Systems — designing an agent that plans, uses tools, and doesn't hallucinate its research, with source verification built in. Week nineteen is Agentic Text-to-SQL — reliable data reasoning, and specifically, how you prevent an agent from ever running a dangerous query against a real production database.
Week twenty is Multi-Agent Coordination — how agents actually communicate and delegate, and critically, how a multi-agent system knows when to stop, so it doesn't loop forever or blow up your cost. Week twenty-one is Self-Improving Agents — systems that generate a fix, test it, and refine it, inside a sandboxed environment with rollback.
Week twenty-two is where it gets specifically FDE: Decomposition and Case Study Interviews. This is the single most distinctive round in an FDE interview loop — it originated at Palantir, and today it's used at OpenAI, Anthropic, Glean, Salesforce, and Databricks. You'll work through a library of ten-plus real case scenarios across fintech, healthcare, defense, and enterprise SaaS, and you'll learn the specific ways candidates fail this round — jumping to a solution before framing the problem properly, missing the data picture entirely, not anchoring your scope to actual evals. This week also includes the AI-assisted pair-coding interview round, using Claude Code from week twelve, and a system design round built specifically around agentic and RAG architectures.
Week twenty-three is Behavioral and Procurement-Security Interviews — sixteen FDE-specific behavioral prompts across eight categories: customer disagreement, a live deployment incident, navigating an org chart, escalation moments. And something genuinely unique to this program: a procurement and security simulation, where a hostile ‘security officer’ cross-examines you on data residency, audit trails, vendor risk, prompt-injection mitigation. In a real FDE process, this round exists, and almost nobody walks in prepared for it. The program closes out through week twenty-four with placement support, your final decision-log entry, a portfolio walkthrough, and planning your first ninety days in an actual FDE role.
